catalog_quote: 2.1.1. General features of vowels ... Most of the adjectival roots and verbal roots have lengthened allophones. Moreover, the length contrasts are typically found in medial position. It is possible that the contrast is a matter of stress rather than in length in the case of adjectives, but this possibility has not been fully investigatied yet. ... 2.3. Supra-segmental Phonemes 2.3.1. Nasalization Nasalization is phonemic in Rongpo. Any vowel followed or preceded by a nasal consonant is automatically nasalized and it is not marked. But phonemic nasalization is heavier than the automatic nasalization. ... 2.3.2. Tones We have established a two tone system for Rongpo, but it is difficult to find true minimal pairs to show the contrasts. new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule for word-stress placement is given. The sketch treats Rongpo as a two-tone language (high falling vs unmarked level, with tone alternations in imperative forms) and lists only nasalization and tone as supra-segmental phonemes; the sole mention of stress is the speculation that the medial vowel-length contrast in adjectives might really be stress, left uninvestigated.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Tone: high falling may surface as level and vice versa in certain constructions, e.g. /t»appəŋ/ 'to beat' vs imperatives /tad/, /tɛni/; /thiŋpəŋ/ 'to spread' level but imperatives /th»iŋ/, /th»iŋni/ high falling.
new_statements.domain_note: Word/morpheme level; Marcha dialect data (informant from Chinka village, Chamoli). Printed SER 19 wording differs trivially from the born-digital file ('rather than length', 'fully investigated'); SER 19 scanned renders 'falling' as 'fa11ing'.
new_statements.identity_note: Sharma 2001 describes the Marcha (Marchha) dialect of the Mana/Niti valleys, Chamoli (informant from Chinka village); he states Marcha and Tolcha differ only phonetically. Glottolog rong1264 = Rongpo covers both; WALS 'Marchha' (mrc) maps to rong1264. Distinct from Rangkas of Johar (LSI 'Rangkas or Saukiya Khun'), which is a separate Almora-group language. Glottolog ref 557422 ('Sharma 2003, in Thurgood & LaPolla, The Sino-Tibetan Languages, pp. 9-77') appears to be a misattributed record of the same sketch as it appears in LaPolla (ed.) 2001, The Tibeto-Burman Languages of Uttar Pradesh, pp. 9-72, not a separate work.
